title: Knowledge Check 3: Lessons 17-24
description: Questions pooled from Lessons 17-24 of the agentic-ai series. Score 80% or higher to progress toward the practice exam.

questions.question: An agent reads a document from an outside source, and hidden instructions inside that document try to redirect it. Why is this kind of prompt injection hard to stop by filtering what the user typed?
options: It arrives on content the agent retrieves itself.
The model obeys only text the user types directly.
Input filters inspect only the final answer produced.
Retrieved text is hashed before the model reads it.
questions.explanation: Indirect injection rides in on content the agent retrieves itself, so the hostile text travels the same legitimate path as the task; blocking it at the input layer would block the agent's work.

questions.question: Why does keeping a longer list of blocked phrases fail to make an agent secure against prompt injection?
options: Blocked-phrase lists only matter when the agent has no tools attached.
The model is stochastic, so any fixed blocklist can be reformulated around.
A static phrase list is far too costly to check on every single request.
An attacker can read the list of blocked phrases and then disable it entirely.
questions.explanation: The model is a stochastic predictor, not a deterministic parser, so any fixed filter only catches attacks already known and attackers can always reformulate.

questions.question: Once you accept that the model itself may be fooled, where does the most durable defense against a successful prompt injection live?
options: In a stricter system prompt and more safety training.
In containment of what the agent can reach and do.
In a longer list of blocked input phrases.
In retraining the model on safe examples.
questions.explanation: The model layer is probabilistic and can be fooled; the durable defense is a deterministic boundary that limits what the agent can reach and do, so a fooled model still cannot act freely.

questions.question: When you gate which actions an agent may take, why is an allowlist safer than a denylist?
options: An allowlist denies by default, so anything you did not think to list is refused.
An allowlist runs its checks faster than a denylist can at runtime.
A denylist cannot express a rule that blocks more than one value at a time.
A denylist requires the model itself to confirm every blocked action before it runs.
questions.explanation: An allowlist denies by default and fails closed on anything unnamed, while a denylist admits by default and lets through whatever you forgot to list.

questions.question: Why should output validation run its cheapest structural checks before its expensive semantic checks?
options: Semantic checks are deterministic, so they must always run last.
Cheap checks reject most bad output, so the costly pass only sees survivors.
Structural checks would corrupt the output if they ran out of order.
The model can only ever be invoked one single time for each response it produces.
questions.explanation: Running cheap structural checks first rejects most bad output at almost no cost, so the expensive semantic pass only runs on what survives.

questions.question: What is a required property of a safe refusal path when the output gate rejects a response?
options: It always retries generation until the gate finally passes.
It shows the user the exact validation error that fired.
It returns a neutral message and logs the detailed reason separately.
It forwards the rejected output straight to the downstream system regardless.
questions.explanation: A safe refusal returns a neutral message with no echo of the rejected content and logs the detailed reason out of band, so it neither leaks data nor helps an attacker.

questions.question: An eval scores a wrong but padded answer higher than a correct but concise one. Which judge bias explains this?
options: Position bias.
Self-enhancement bias.
Verbosity bias.
The domain gap.
questions.explanation: Verbosity bias makes a judge favor longer output, so a padded wrong answer can outscore a correct concise one unless the rubric rewards conciseness.

questions.question: Before trusting an automated judge to gate releases, what should you do first?
options: Run it against human-reviewed labels and measure how often it agrees.
Raise its temperature so that the scores vary a good deal more.
Ask the judge to evaluate its own previous scores for consistency.
Replace it with the exact-match metrics that it was originally meant to replace.
questions.explanation: A judge is a probabilistic instrument, so you validate it against human-reviewed labels and measure agreement before letting it gate anything.

questions.question: Why does a good evaluation set include cases drawn from real production traffic rather than only clean synthetic examples?
options: Synthetic examples are always too long to use inside a gate.
Real traffic carries the edge cases that clean examples miss.
Production data never contains any personal or sensitive information at all.
A judge can only score inputs that it has already seen before.
questions.explanation: Datasets built only from documentation or synthetic generation come out too clean and miss the edge cases and adversarial inputs real users produce.

questions.question: An agent returns a wrong answer and you need to see which step caused it. What does a trace give you that a dashboard of averages does not?
options: The specific run's sequence of model calls, tool calls, and retrievals.
A guarantee that the failing run will never happen again.
The original training data that the model was built from many months ago.
A lower average latency across all of the recent runs.
questions.explanation: A trace records the specific run's steps in order, which is what lets you find the one run that made the wrong decision instead of reading an average.

questions.question: Why are prompt and response bodies left out of standard telemetry spans by default?
options: They are too large for any telemetry backend to store.
They routinely contain sensitive data, so capturing them is opt-in.
They change too often to standardize the attribute names.
They are only useful for training a model, never for debugging a run.
questions.explanation: Prompt and completion text routinely contains sensitive data, so content capture is an opt-in event rather than a default span attribute.

questions.question: What makes a structured log record useful for diagnosing an agent run?
options: It is printed as a human-readable sentence with no fixed fields.
It is written only once, at the very end of the run.
It carries a run identifier that links it back to its trace.
It stores the full prompt on every line by default.
questions.explanation: A structured record with named fields and a run identifier can be joined back to its trace, turning a log line into a pointer to the full context.

questions.question: When comparing agent frameworks, which factors actually reveal the differences between them?
options: Their GitHub star counts and their overall popularity in the developer community.
Their orchestration model, state management, and communication pattern.
The length and polish of their marketing pages on the web.
The number of contributors listed on their public repositories.
questions.explanation: The three coordination axes, orchestration model, state management, and communication pattern, are the real differences; popularity and marketing are noise on top.

questions.question: What design feature lets a graph runtime support retries, pause-and-resume, and time-travel debugging?
options: A prompt that tells the model to remember its state.
A larger context window on the underlying model.
A shared, typed, checkpointable state object.
A team of role-based agents with backstories.
questions.explanation: The runtime persists a shared, typed state through checkpointing, which is what enables retries, pause-and-resume, and time-travel debugging.

questions.question: An agent needs to read files, run shell commands, and edit code directly. Which framework design best matches that need?
options: A role-based crew where each member owns a task.
A small handoff-oriented SDK with hosted tools.
An integration ecosystem for chaining components.
A framework that gives the agent a computer.
questions.explanation: The Claude Agent SDK is built to give the agent a computer, exposing built-in file, shell, and edit tools, which matches an agent that works over a filesystem.

questions.question: In a hand-built agent loop, what is the model's role when it decides to use a tool?
options: It executes the tool and reads the result directly.
It proposes a tool call that the surrounding code runs and returns.
It writes the tool's source code before it calls it.
It skips the rest of the loop and returns a final answer straight away.
questions.explanation: The model only proposes a tool call; the surrounding code executes it and feeds the result back, so the model never runs a tool itself.

questions.question: When feeding tool results back into a conversation, what has to happen first for the API to accept the request?
options: The tool results must always be appended before the assistant's tool-call message.
The system prompt must be rewritten on every single turn.
The model must be told that the tool call failed.
The assistant's tool-call message must be appended before the tool results.
questions.explanation: Each tool result references a tool_call_id that must already exist, so the assistant message carrying the tool calls has to be appended before the results.

questions.question: In the canonical agent loop, what signal tells the code that the agent is done?
options: A response that contains only plain text and no tool calls.
A response that contains at least one tool call for the code to run.
A response that exceeds the token budget for the run.
A response that repeats a previous tool call it already made.
questions.explanation: A text-only response is the termination signal; a response with tool calls is the continuation signal that keeps the loop running.

questions.question: What distinguishes ReAct from a plain tool-calling loop?
options: It skips tool calls entirely and answers straight from the model's memory.
It interleaves reasoning with each action and observation.
It plans the entire task once before acting.
It runs several agents in parallel.
questions.explanation: ReAct interleaves a natural-language reasoning trace with each action and observation, so the model reasons before it acts instead of firing tools blindly.

questions.question: Why does plan-and-execute often make fewer large-model calls than a ReAct-style agent?
options: It never calls any tools at all.
It re-plans after every single action it takes.
It splits planning from doing, so steps run on cheaper models.
It evaluates its own output against the original request before it answers.
questions.explanation: Plan-and-execute separates planning from doing, so the large model is called for planning and re-planning while individual steps can run on cheaper models.

questions.question: Which pattern adds an evaluate-and-revise pass so an agent can learn from a failed first attempt?
options: ReAct.
Plan-and-execute.
The plain tool loop.
Reflection.
questions.explanation: Reflection adds an actor, an evaluator, and a self-reflection step that scores a trajectory and feeds verbal feedback into the next attempt.

questions.question: What makes the orchestrator-worker pattern different from plain parallelization?
options: Subtasks are decided at runtime after the orchestrator sees the input.
The workers all share one single central context window.
The subtasks are fixed in code before the run even starts.
The workers run strictly one at a time in a fixed, preplanned sequence.
questions.explanation: In orchestrator-worker the orchestrator decides the subtasks at runtime after seeing the specific input, unlike plain parallelization where the split is fixed in code.

questions.question: Multi-agent debate does not divide labor. What does it add instead?
options: Faster throughput for high-volume requests.
Redundancy: several instances cross-examine each other.
A single coordinator that routes each task to one specialist agent.
A cheaper way to run many small independent tasks.
questions.explanation: Debate adds redundancy rather than division of labor: several instances cross-examine each other so a confident wrong answer can be caught.

questions.question: What is the recommended approach to reaching for a multi-agent design?
options: Always use several agents for any real task.
Prefer it whenever more than one model is available.
Start simple and add coordination only when a single agent pays a real cost.
Use a coordinator whenever a task can be broken into any number of separate steps.
questions.explanation: Start with the simplest single agent and add coordination only when you can point to a real cost it is paying, since every extra agent adds nondeterminism and cost.
